bibliography.abstract: Urban digital twins are increasingly shaping the future of urban planning and management, offering new opportunities for more informed, efficient, and sustainable cities. However, research on their development, applications, and challenges remains geographically uneven, raising important questions about digital inequalities and the diversity of urban contexts represented in the literature. This study analyses 2,650 Scopus-indexed publications from 2001 to 2026 to explore thematic and geographical patterns in urban digital twin research. Using topic modelling, 26 topics were identified and grouped into five challenge dimensions: Technical-Infrastructural, Sectoral-Application, Foundational-Integrative, Institutional-Governance, and Security-Trust. Despite rapid growth in publication volume, only 29.3% of studies are grounded in real-city case studies, with limited evidence of improvement over time. Technical-Infrastructural and Sectoral-Application research dominate the literature, while Institutional-Governance and Security-Trust receive comparatively less attention. Clear geographical differences also emerge, with Asia showing a stronger Technical-Infrastructural emphasis and Europe a greater focus on Sectoral-Application research. Africa and Oceania demonstrate relatively high proportions of Institutional-Governance research, although their small samples limit broader generalisation. The findings highlight persistent geographical imbalances in the visibility, thematic priorities, and empirical grounding of urban digital twin research. By identifying these divides, the study provides a foundation for more geographically inclusive, institutionally informed, and context-sensitive research, with implications for the future integration of digital twins into urban planning and governance.
bibliography.title: The global geography of urban digital twin research: patterns and divides

en.caveats: Small publication samples from Africa and Oceania restrict the generalizability of thematic trends identified in those regions.
en.what: An analysis of 2,650 Scopus-indexed publications from 2001 to 2026 used topic modelling to extract 26 themes in urban digital twin research across five core dimensions: Technical-Infrastructural, Sectoral-Application, Foundational-Integrative, Institutional-Governance, and Security-Trust. Only 29.3% of the analyzed publications ground their work in real-city case studies, with Technical-Infrastructural and Sectoral-Application topics dominating the literature. Geographical patterns show Asia prioritizing technical infrastructure while Europe leads in sectoral applications, alongside severe overall regional sample imbalances.
en.why: It proves that despite the rapid expansion of urban digital twin scholarship, the field remains overwhelmingly theoretical and regionally polarized, lacking empirical validation in real-world urban environments.
